rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods, Modeling Framework and Results, Table 2 <U+2013> the authors build and run their own basin-scale hydroeconomic optimization model of the Upper Rio Grande (EBID, 89,000 acres) for drip subsidy scenarios 0-100%.
rows.notes: The study's own result on this claim is a model output only: Table 2 shows aquifer storage gains falling from 74,000 to 40,000 acre-feet/yr and aquifer-to-river gains from 32,000 to 17,000 as drip subsidy rises, because drip deep percolation is set to 0 in the input data (Table 1). The only comparison with observations is that the base-case technology share (~90% flood, <10% drip) 'corresponds approximately' to actual 2006 EBID conditions; recharge, return flow and depletion outputs are never checked against measurements, and the counterfactual subsidy scenarios cannot be. Under the rule that an unvalidated model is not own evidence, Q2 is answered no; this is the main doubt.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results, Tables 2-3 <U+2013> own hydroeconomic optimization model runs for the Rio Grande Basin under 11 drip subsidy levels.
rows.notes: The model predicts a rebound: total irrigated land rises from 75,000 to 87,000 acres (Table 3), ET/depletion rises from 167,000 to 204,000 acre-feet (Table 2), and 'total water conserved' becomes negative (-36,700 acre-feet/yr at 100% subsidy), i.e. water saved on-farm is reinvested in more acreage and higher-yield crops. However this is a simulation whose outputs for depletion, acreage expansion and return flows are not compared with measurements from the basin (only the base-case technology share is said to roughly match 2006 EBID conditions). Treated as not own validated evidence per the model rule.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results <U+2013> own basin-scale optimization model runs (Tables 2 and 3).
rows.notes: The passage's content matches the study's modeled result: as drip subsidies rise, water applied falls (364,000 to 324,000 acre-feet) while acreage (75,000 to 87,000 acres), yields and total consumptive use/ET (167,000 to 204,000 acre-feet) increase. But the result is a model output built on assumed per-crop ET and deep-percolation coefficients (Table 1) and is not validated against observed depletion or acreage change; only the base-case land-use pattern is loosely compared with 2006 conditions. Q2 therefore no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results <U+2013> own hydroeconomic model of the Rio Grande Basin.
rows.notes: The study models reduced downstream delivery (314,000 to 292,000 acre-feet, Table 2) and reduced aquifer-river gains with more drip, and in Conclusions states that reduced return flows 'could impair existing water right holders'. The impairment of right holders is an inference discussed from model outputs, not a modeled or measured outcome, and the model outputs themselves are not compared with observations of the real system. Q2 no.

rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and Methods and Results <U+2013> own basin-scale model runs reported in Tables 2 and 3.
rows.notes: Reduced return flows/aquifer gains and lower downstream deliveries under drip subsidies are model outputs (Table 2); the complication of water governance and water rights administration is discussed in the Conclusions as a policy implication, not modeled or observed. Model outputs are not compared with measurements from the basin (only an approximate base-case match of flood/drip shares). Q2 no.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a primary modeling study (dynamic nonlinear hydroeconomic optimization, 20-year horizon, annual time step) of drip irrigation subsidies in the Rio Grande Basin. All rows are rated Q2 'no' because the model's results on return flows, recharge, depletion and acreage expansion are not compared with measurements from the real system; the only check is a qualitative statement that the base-case technology share roughly matches 2006 EBID conditions. If a reader accepts that as validation, rows 1-3 could be Q2 'yes' with Q6 'yes' (irrigation district scale) and Q7 'yes' (effect conditional on return flows being reusable rather than lost to saline sinks, footnote **), with Q3, Q4 (return flow/aquifer seepage are modeled intermediate variables, arguably yes), Q5 and Q9 'no'.
